power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: PsycInfo, and PsycArticles including quantitative and qualitative reports published up to March 28 th , 2026.

Qualitative reports were coded according to the five-factor model of substance use motives assigning material to the dimensions of enhancement, coping, expansion, conformity, social and other motives.
Results: A total of 50 articles were included.
Three survey studies were identified that reported enhancement as the major motivational drive.
In contrast, the qualitative reports contained coping motives as the most prominent drive.
Enhancement and expansion motives were also reported, while social and conformity motives were nearly absent from the qualitative literature.

Discussion: The non-medical use of N2O is related to a diverse array of motivational forces, with enhancement and coping with negative psychological and physical sensations appearing to be particularly relevant.
Recreational non-problematic use seems to be dominated by enhancement motives, while escalated and use with adverse consequences is more strongly related to coping motives.

As systematic assessments with validated instruments regarding the motivational drives behind N2O use are lacking, further research is needed to make reliable statements about the motive profile of N2O.

Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a colourless and sweet-smelling gas with an established role in anaesthesia, analgesia, anxiolysis during medical interventions, dental procedures, during childbirth, and emergency medicine (1) (2) (3).
text.formatted: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a colourless and sweet-smelling gas with an established role in anaesthesia, analgesia, anxiolysis during medical interventions, dental procedures, during childbirth, and emergency medicine <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(3)</ref>.

text.text: For recreational use, the substance is of interest primarily because of its psychoactive effects.
Subjective effects include euphoria, dream-like states, distortion of temporal and spatial perception, and acoustic and optical illusions and hallucinations (4) (5) (6) (7).
text.formatted: Subjective effects include euphoria, dream-like states, distortion of temporal and spatial perception, and acoustic and optical illusions and hallucinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Potential adverse effects include dizziness, nausea, vomiting, dissociation, disorientation, numbness and weakness, as well as impairment of cognitive, psychomotor and memory-based performance (7).
text.formatted: Potential adverse effects include dizziness, nausea, vomiting, dissociation, disorientation, numbness and weakness, as well as impairment of cognitive, psychomotor and memory-based performance <ref type="bibr">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Use over a longer period of time or in large quantities can be associated with significant health consequences.
This includes nerve damage such as polyneuropathies and myelopathy due to vitamin B12 deficiency (8) (9) (10) (11).

text.text: While the increase of non-medical use and associated health consequences is well documented, there is a lack of explanatory approaches for these developments.

Therefore, we aim to implement a motivational perspective that may help explain N2O use patterns. Cox & Klinger (26) posited a fundamental motivational model of substance use based on the pursuit of positive incentives and the avoidance of negative ones in order to maximize positive affective changes.

text.text: The decision to use a psychoactive drug is therefore a motivational one and is made by weighing the expected emotional consequences of use against the expected affective changes caused by refraining from use (26, 27).

text.text: Since its publication, the motivational model of (originally alcohol) use has been adapted and expanded to account for motives for the use of other substances, incorporating substance specific subjective and pharmacological effects.
Jones and colleagues (28) developed a four-factor model for use motives of prescription opioids.

text.text: Due to the pharmacological effects and the associated physical stimulus of pain management, pain was added as a motive and thus replaced conformity motives that seem to be less relevant for this group of substances (28).

text.text: For cannabis use, the model was extended by the addition of an expansion motive, which captures the consciousness-expanding and perception-altering components as incentives for use.

This fivefactor model explained additional variance in use compared to the original model (29) and has been successfully applied to analyse the motivational drives of psychedelic substances (30), which are similar to N2O in terms of the subjective effect profile.

text.text: As substance use motives have repeatedly been shown to predict alcohol use (27, 31, 32), cannabis use (31), treatment response in substance use disorders (SUDs) (33), as well as development of a SUD (34), they might also be relevant for explaining N2O use patterns.

text.text: The five-factor approach of substance use motives may therefore provide a helpful framework for the assessment of non-medical N2O use.
However, to date this framework has not been systematically applied to investigate N2O use motives.

Thus, the aim of the present review is to systematically survey the existing literature on the motives for non-medical use of N2O in order to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying motivational drives of N2O use and their association with use patterns.

text.text: Studies and reports that reported or collected data on explicit motives for the non-medical use of N2O by one or more people were included.
Studies in which N2O use was part of a medical procedure were excluded.
This includes studies in which N2O was used as part of scientific trials or as part of medical or dental procedures for analgesia or anaesthesia.
No further restrictions were made on the population in terms of age, sex, medical history, or other sociodemographic variables.
Studies involving animals were excluded, as the aim of this review was to investigate motives for human N2O use.
Given the nature of the research question, no comparison group was included.
Studies and reports had to be published in English or German.
Furthermore, reports, abstracts, and posters prepared and published in the context of conferences were excluded.
At the level of study design and publication time frame, no restrictions were applied, as limited available data was assumed.
This systematic review was carried out in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (37).
The data was obtained by searching in bibliographic databases PubMed (MEDLINE), EMBASE, Web of Science, and PubPsych.
The simultaneous search of the PsycInfo and PsycArticles databases was carried out via the EBSCOhost platform.
The search algorithm followed Boolean logic and the search terms were connected accordingly with Boolean operators.

Qualitative reports of use motives, such as case reports or interview analyses, were extracted as citations and assigned to the five-factor model of substance use dimensions: conformity, coping, enhancement, expansion, and social motives.

Each study was coded with "1" if a motive was reported and "0" if the corresponding motive was not present and performed by two independent coders (AES and LAB).

More than one motive could be coded per study.

text.text: A previously unreported facet of the motivation to consume is inhalation in connection with masturbation as reported in three case reports of men aged 29 to 35 (83,84,86).
In this systematic review, we examined the use motives for the non-medical use of N2O.

The central finding of this review is that the number of studies on this topic is considerably limited and distinguished by a lack of systematic investigations using standardized questionnaires of substance use motives.
Only three systematic surveys were found which converge on enhancement as the most prominent use motive.
The results of merged qualitative reports showed a different distribution pattern.
Here, coping motives were mentioned most frequently, followed by the highly heterogeneous category of Other Motives.
Enhancement and expansion motives formed the third and fourth largest motive groups.
Social motives and use out of conformity hardly played a role in the included reports.
Interestingly the reported motives in systematic surveys differed from the results of the qualitative reports.
Specifically, the quantitative survey studies (41) (42) (43) reported enhancement as the most prominent use motive, in line with previous literature (90).
text.formatted: Specifically, the quantitative survey studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(41)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(42)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(43)</ref> reported enhancement as the most prominent use motive, in line with previous literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(90)</ref>.

text.text: However, qualitative reports mostly contained use motives related to dealing with negative physical and psychological sensations such as stress management and self-medication.
Thus, qualitative reports contain coping as the most prominent motive.

This difference is likely due to selection bias, as a large proportion of the people interviewed in the qualitative reports had to seek medical treatment due to the negative consequences of their severe N2O use.
The systematic surveys in comparison contained reports from convenience and student samples without any medical indication.

This difference in pattern suggests that people with problematic use behaviour tend to use N2O out of coping motives, while people with unproblematic use behaviour are more likely to report enhancement and expansion motives which is in line with general literature on use motives in SUDs (91) (92) (93).

For example, N2O use to manage depressed mood or withdrawal symptoms is reflected by clinical trials using N2O to treat these symptoms (94, 95).

text.text: However, since the effects of N2O are only short-lasting, this motive was initially not considered as a primary motive for non-medical use.
Social motives and use out of conformity were reported by very few individuals in the qualitative reports while being a prominent motive in quantitative surveys.

text.text: Indeed, N2O is often inhaled at parties in private environments, a context of use that includes many social interactions.
As such the recreational non-coping use is often related to group pressures (19) and often occurs through friends and social groups (80, 97).

text.text: The recreational users, without severe problematic use and rare coping motives seem to be more strongly influenced by social contexts and social use motives.
In comparison, N2O use with a problematic, coping-related use motive, might be of a more solitary nature providing less social pressure but at the same time less opportunity for social control.

In addition to the motives subsumed under the traditional motivational model of substance use, the qualitative reports contained specific use motives that might have been overlooked in previous literature.

First, specifically for young adults and adolescents boredom was associated frequently with N2O use (18, 58, 79, 80), in line with previous literature on psychoactive substance use among young people in general (98).

text.text: Second, the use of N2O in the context of autoerotic activities was an unexpected addition.
As this motivational drive was only reported in qualitative reports related to medical emergencies, there was no indication in the included literature with regard to the prevalence of this practice.

text.text: Fourth, we report two cases of using N2O as a sleeping aid which has rarely been mentioned outside of the studies included here, apart from individual cases among dentists (99).

These diverse motivational facets in addition to the lack of systematic research and differential findings related to the classic motivational dimensions of substance use highlight that N2O use is not easily assigned to a specific motivational drive.
Indeed, our review highlights a diverse landscape of motivations that can drive N2O use.

In relation to the question of increases in N2O use and corresponding health issues our review on one hand supports previous findings that increased use among young people might be specifically related to a desire for enhancement (100) and a desire to deal with boredom (101).

text.text: On the other hand, we also report a high frequency of coping motives and issues related to problematic use.

Our results suggest that the userbase of N2O is not a homogeneous group solely consisting of young people using for enhancement purposes but contains a wide variety of people of all ages and motivational drives which supports a therapeutic approach marked by respect for individual circumstances (e.g., harm reduction psychotherapy (102, 103)).

text.text: Thus, an appropriate response to N2O in terms of prevention and clinical settings should be flexible insofar as being able to incorporate and deal with heterogeneous motivational drives.

Most importantly however, is a proper research literature that systematically assesses use motives using established measures in combination with qualitative methods to provide a solid database of relevant use motives across the diverse userbase of N2O.
First, a general limitation of the significance of use motives is the recording of the theoretical construct via retrospective reports.
Recent research shows that motives assessed via ambulatory assessment might differ substantially from retrospective reports (104) (105) (106).

text.text: This literature implies that retrospective measurements are less about the motivation present at the moment of use, but rather about attributions that the person makes about themselves with regard to their use.
Specifically, the attributions may be subject to memory errors and excessive attention to negative emotions, which could lead to more frequent reports of coping motives (104).

text.text: Additionally, retrospective reports might represent an average of use motives across all use situations, while ambulatory assessments capture state motives that are present in the respective specific situation and shed light on the variance of use motives within the person (27).

text.text: Second, extracted use motives from case reports were mostly collected in the course of history taking in medical settings.

Since the use of psychoactive substances is stigmatized and these conversations took place in person, unlike an anonymous survey of students, responses may have been influenced by social desirability or contextual factors.
Additionally, the responses were documented according to the interpretation and understanding of the respective questioner.
All of which might distort the reliability of reported use motives.
Nonetheless, these case reports offered a unique data source underlining the heterogenous nature of N2O use motives and are a valuable contribution to this understudied field.
Third, the coding of the case reports was based on the motivational model of substance use which limited the available categories for coding.
On the one hand this limited the number of available categories and led to our second-largest category being Other motives.
On the other hand, this model provided a useful structure to compare case reports with systematic survey results.
Additionally, this allowed us to identify a number of additional use motives that do not fall into the classical structure and thus highlights the diversity of N2O users.
Finally, the contributions included in the analysis differ in their quality and methods.

The studies included in the review are only of limited use to provide a representative answer to the question of the motives for N2O use, as none of these studies identified the recording of motives as the primary goal and none used a standardised measure for this purpose.
With the exception of the exploratory interviews by Nabben and colleagues (80) the exploration of use motives was a secondary goal.
This highlights again the need for systematic research on this issue.
The results of this review compile the findings of the currently existing research on use motives of non-medical use of N2O and point to a research gap on this topic.
This is the only review on this question to date and the results are to be understood as an exploratory analysis due to the very limited literature on the topic.

Based on our results we report that N2O is consumed for a variety of reasons, including enhancement motives, such as the search for euphoria, intoxication and new experiences, but also to cope with negative psychological and physical sensations.
Specifically, enhancement motives seem more pronounced in N2O users without problematic use, while coping motives seem to play a larger role in problematic N2O use.
However, systematic research on use motives across the heterogenous population of N2O users and use of appropriate wellestablished measures is still lacking.
